title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, and Runbooks
author: Priya Natarajan
body:
Overview

This document is the canonical team wiki and playbook for Redwood Inference's Serving Runtime. It consolidates the runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, known issues and mitigations, release notes highlights, and operational runbooks. Intended audience: serving runtime engineers, SREs, performance engineers, and on-call rotation.

Goals

- Provide a single reference for architecture and operational patterns.
- Capture kernel scheduling rules and heuristics used in production.
- Define profiling and benchmarking procedures that produce repeatable metrics.
- Record common issues, workarounds, and ownership for fast on-call resolution.

Contents

1) Runtime Architecture Overview
2) Kernel Scheduling Design and Heuristics
3) Profiling Playbook (how to profile end-to-end requests)
4) Benchmarking Suite and CI Integration
5) Release Notes (recent highlights)
6) Known Issues and Mitigations
7) Runbooks and Oncall Procedures
8) Team Wiki Links and Ownership

---

1) Runtime Architecture Overview

Summary:
The Serving Runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine deployed across hosted, dedicated, and private modes. Core components: request router, worker pool (GRPC service per GPU), kernel executor, KV cache, batching manager, and metrics/tracing pipeline. The runtime prioritizes predictable tail latency and throughput via continuous batching, prefix caching and adaptive kernel selection.

High-level data flow:

- Client request -> Frontend (API edge) -> Router
- Router consults routing policy (latency SLA, cost tier, model compatibility)
- Request dispatched to Worker Pool -> Batcher -> Kernel Executor -> Token stream -> Response

Key design choices:

- Continuous Batching: Batcher aggregates in-flight token generation work until per-request latency budget or batch size triggers.
- KV Cache: Per-session KV caches persisted in local memory with optional Redis-backed warm start for long-tail sessions.
- Kernel Selection: Model profile + sequence length distribution drives selection of attention kernel, matmul kernel and quantization path at request time.
- Graceful Fallbacks: Router can redirect to lower-cost/compatibility models on capacity pressure; fallback policies are defined per-customer and per-route.

Service map (abbreviated):

| Service | Responsibility | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| router | routing, policy enforcement, fallbacks | runtime-router-team |
| worker | GPU inference, batching, kernel exec | serving-runtime |
| kv-cache | session caching & eviction | serving-runtime |
| trace-exporter | metrics/traces to observability backend | infra-observability |

SLOs and Targets (production):

- 99th percentile token latency: <= 250ms for shortest-context routes
- Availability: 99.95% per-region for hosted API endpoints
- Median tokens/sec per GPU: target depends on model class (see benchmarking table below)

---

2) Kernel Scheduling Design and Heuristics

Objective: select kernels and schedule work to GPUs to maximize throughput subject to latency SLOs and memory constraints. The scheduler operates in two stages: static placement and dynamic scheduling.

Static placement rules:

- Pin large-model weights to a single GPU with sharded optimizer states (for training-mode tasks) — inference uses full model replica unless model supports tensor-parallel inference.
- Reserve 1-2GB headroom per GPU for KV cache growth and meta structures.

Dynamic scheduling heuristics (used by scheduler v3):

- Priority buckets: realtime < interactive < batch. Realtime requests preempt batch windows.
- Batch sizing heuristic: target_batch = clamp( floor( L * R ), 1, B_max ) where L is average request length, R is target concurrency factor, B_max is configured per-GPU model limit.
- Kernel specialization: for attention, prefer fused attention kernels for seq_len <= 2048; switch to memory-efficient attention for seq_len > 2048.
- Quantization path selection: auto-switch to int8 kernel when model quantization profile exists and quality regression checks pass on last 3 eval runs.
- Backpressure: if queuing time > latency_budget * 0.6, reduce new batch formation and open fast-path preemption.

Tunable parameters (config file: /etc/runtime/scheduler-config.yaml)

| param | description | example |
| scheduler.window_ms | base batching window | 6 |
| scheduler.burst_concurrency | extra concurrency allowed during bursts | 2 |
| scheduler.seq_threshold | seq length to switch kernels | 2048 |
| scheduler.quant_min_score | min eval quality score to allow quant path | 0.985 |

Example CLI to view current scheduler state:

$ rictl runtime scheduler status --node gpu-12

Outputs: active-batches, queue-depth, kernel-path, recent-preemptions

---

3) Profiling Playbook

Purpose: reproduce high-latency requests, identify hotspots (kernel, memcpy, serialization), and propose mitigations.

When to run profiling:

- 99th percentile token latency regression > 15% over baseline
- New model onboarding where profile not previously recorded
- Unexplained increase in GPU utilization or tail latency spikes

Step-by-step profiling procedure:

1. Reproduce workload in staging using the production trace sampler. Use the same model version and config.
2. Collect flamegraphs and timeline traces:
   - CPU: perf + eBPF (capture syscalls, scheduling).
   - GPU: NVIDIA Nsight or ROCm rocprof for kernel timings and memcpy metrics.
   - Runtime: enable detailed request tracing (rictl runtime trace start <trace-id> --level debug).
3. Correlate traces with metrics: token-per-second, batch sizes, queue times, kernel durations.
4. Identify top-3 hotspots and classify: compute-bound, memory-bound, serialization-bound, or queueing.
5. Run microbenchmarks for suspect kernels with our micro-bench harness: /opt/bench/kerntest --model gpt-3b --kernel attention-fused --seq 512 --steps 1000
6. Apply mitigation (one at a time) and re-run profiler:
   - increase batching window by +2ms (if compute-bound and latency SLO allows)
   - switch to alternative kernel (e.g., memory-efficient attention)
   - adjust CUDA stream concurrency or NCCL settings
   - enable KV cache warmup for long sessions
7. Document results in the profiling ticket and update model profile record.

Artifacts to capture and attach to ticket:

- flamegraphs (CPU & GPU)
- kernel timeline CSV (timestamp, kernel, duration_ns, stream)
- batch formation histogram
- before/after SLO percentiles

---

4) Benchmarking Suite and CI Integration

Overview:
The benchmarking suite verifies throughput and cost targets for each model class and hardware SKU. Bench jobs are run: on PRs for kernel/runtime changes (smoke), nightly for fleet-wide regressions, and on-demand as part of model onboarding.

Repository and CI jobs:
- repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/serving-benchmarks.git
- smoke job: bench/smoke.yml (runs 3 short throughputs across two model sizes)
- nightly job: bench/nightly.yml (full regression across models and SKUs)

Key metrics captured:

- tokens/sec per GPU (median, p95)
- p50/p95/p99 token latency
- GPU utilization and memory headroom
- cost-per-1M tokens (estimated)

Example benchmark config (bench/configs/gpt-family.yaml):

model: gpt-3b
batch_sizes: [1, 4, 8, 16]
seq_lengths: [64, 256, 512]
gpu_skus: [a100-80gb, h100-80gb]
runs_per_config: 5

Interpreting results:
- Flag any change where p95 latency increases > 10% or tokens/sec decreases > 7% relative to baseline commit.
- CI will open a regression issue with artifacts and attach profiling trace.

Bench governance:
- Baseline commit is tagged as bench-baseline/YYYY-MM-DD in the repo.
- Owners: perf-eng and serving-runtime. Bench failures require triage within 48 hours.

---

5) Release Notes (recent highlights)

2026-10-01 (v3.4.0):
- Kernel scheduler v3 deployed to production regions (US-W, EU-C). Features: priority buckets and preemptive fast-path; observed 12% reduction in p99 latency for interactive routes.
- Default attention kernel now auto-switches at seq_len 2048 to memory-efficient path.
- Added GPU-level tracing export to observability pipeline.

2026-06-15 (v3.2.1):
- KV cache eviction tuning to reduce cache churn for long-running sessions.
- Fix: serialization bug that caused response truncation under specific multi-lingual tokenization conditions.

---

6) Known Issues and Mitigations

Issue: Intermittent p99 latency spikes on a100-80gb during sustained mixed workloads.
- Symptom: p99 spikes 300-700ms, spikes last 30-120 seconds.
- Root cause (investigation): NVLink micro-congestion + large memcpy bursts when KV cache warms.
- Mitigation: Reduce scheduler.window_ms to 4ms for impacted nodes, stagger KV cache warmups by 100ms, and enable memcpy coalescing.
- Long-term: moving to streaming memcpy paths and reducing per-request memcpy footprint.

Issue: Quantized kernel quality regression after automatic rollout.
- Symptom: slight drop (0.8%) in BLEU-like score on internal evals for summarization prompt set.
- Mitigation: automatic rollback to FP16 variant and immediate block on quant paths until three successive eval passes.

For any new significant issue, create an incident ticket and tag sla-impacting=yes. Triage owner is serving-runtime on-call.

---

7) Runbooks and Oncall Procedures

On-call playbook (short):

1. Alert arrives: identify impacted service (router/worker/kv-cache) via alert tags.
2. Run quick health checks: rictl runtime health --node <node> and rictl router status --route <route>.
3. If p99 token latency elevated: check batch sizes (metrics: runtime.batch.size.histogram) and queueing (runtime.queue.depth).
4. If GPU saturating but latency healthy: escalate to perf-eng for kernel tuning.
5. If node-level memory pressure: cordon node and reprovision. Steps:
   a. rictl node cordon gpu-12
   b. rictl cluster drain --node gpu-12 --grace 60s
   c. restart worker service: systemctl restart serving-worker || journalctl -u serving-worker -n 200
6. Post-incident: file postmortem within 72 hours. Include root cause, timeline, and next steps.

Runbook: Fast rollback of problematic kernel rollout:

1. Identify deployment tag: rictl runtime deployments list --model <model>
2. Pin model to previous kernel: rictl runtime model pin --model <model> --version <prev> --reason "rollback - kernel regression"
3. Monitor SLOs for 30 minutes. If stable, promote pin to permanent and create a CR to block auto-rollout.

- Quarterly: full benchmarking sweep across SKUs.
- After every release: run smoke benchmarks and profiling on a holdout region.

Appendix: Quick commands

- View runtime status: rictl runtime status --region us-west1
- Start a detailed trace: rictl runtime trace start --node gpu-12 --duration 60s --level debug --out /tmp/trace-123.zip
- Run kernel microbench: /opt/bench/kerntest --model gpt-3b --kernel attention-fused --seq 256 --steps 500

Contact and feedback

If you find outdated content or missing procedures, open a PR to this page and notify the serving-runtime docs owner (Priya Natarajan). For urgent corrections, file a docs-urgent ticket and ping #docs-owners.
